concept.name: Consumer confidence
concept.definition: A monthly survey-based index of U.S. household attitudes about current business and labor-market conditions and expectations for income, business activity, and jobs, published by The Conference Board with 1985 as the base year (1985=100). It comprises the Present Situation Index and the Expectations Index.
concept.intuition: Confident consumers tend to spend more freely, so the index is watched as a leading indicator of consumption, the largest part of GDP.
concept.mechanics: The Conference Board surveys households online each month (preliminary cutoff around the 22nd), asking five questions on present conditions and six-month expectations; responses are scored, seasonally adjusted, and indexed to the 1985 average of 100, with release at 10 a.m. ET on the last Tuesday of the month.
concept.formula: Consumer Confidence Index = composite of the Present Situation and Expectations indexes, normalized so the 1985 average equals 100.
concept.failure_modes: Sentiment and actual spending can diverge for long stretches - consumers report gloom yet keep spending - and answers are sensitive to headlines such as gasoline prices, stock-market moves, and geopolitical conflict.
concept.misconceptions: It is a survey of attitudes, not a measure of spending itself, and it differs from the University of Michigan's sentiment index, which weights personal finances and inflation expectations differently.
concept.example: In July 2026 the Conference Board Consumer Confidence Index fell 1.4 points to 90.8, with the Present Situation Index at 114.9 and the Expectations Index at 74.7.

citations.source: The Conference Board, Consumer Confidence Survey
citations.section: US Consumer Confidence press release, July 2026
